name: Carla Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm not much of a talker, so you might have to drag it out of me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a blast-hole drill at the Marrow Creek coal mine, open cut. The engineers give us a pattern, a grid of holes, and I drill them to the right depth so the blast crew can load them with explosives. I'm still learning. Last month I drilled a whole row half a metre too shallow and had to go back. I like it because it's the same every day: line up, drill, log the depth, move. What wears me out is the noise through the earmuffs and the night roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe, "Well, that's that," if someone brought it up at lunch. I don't post about stuff online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean I can keep doing what I'm doing. That suits me. I'm not someone who wants things to change every five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep drilling, keep putting 300 a fortnight into the house fund. Nico and I want a deposit in about three years, so I'd just stick to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, maybe, though I wasn't that worried to begin with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you weren't worried to begin with. Is there anything at Marrow Creek that has changed because of new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drills got GPS a couple of years back, before I started. The old guys say it used to be string lines and paint. Now the screen tells you where the hole goes, and I just have to not mess it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the GPS make you feel more or less secure in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never really thought about it. More, I suppose, because it makes the job easier to learn. I'd be worse without it.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe just that's that if someone brought it up at the lunch break. I don't post about things online.
S0.think: Privately it means I can keep doing what I'm doing, which suits me fine. I'm not someone who wants things to change every five minutes.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and keeps putting 300 a fortnight into the house deposit fund. Sticks to the plan of buying with her partner Nico in about three years.
S0.quote: Now the screen tells you where the hole goes, and I just have to not mess it up.
S0.fieldNote: She is quiet and literal, and needed short prompts to open up. Routine is what she likes about the job, and this picture protects it. She has a clear money plan, a house deposit in three years, which anchors everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, "We'll see." There's always talk about the next big thing coming to the mine, and most of it comes slower than people say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the drills would be among the first to go automatic. There are already drills that run themselves at some mines, you just watch them from a screen. I'd be on the list, being junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd wait and see what Marrow Creek actually did before I did anything. I'd bump the savings up to 400 a fortnight, just in case, and cut back on takeaway. I wouldn't start looking elsewhere until something was in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they offered you training to supervise a self-driving drill from a screen, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. But I'd hate it. I'm bad with computers. I can feel when the drill bit hits a soft patch through my seat, and a screen can't give me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it cost you your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know if blame is the word. Companies cut costs, that's what they do. I'd be annoyed, but I wouldn't be marching about it.

S1.say: I'd say we'll see, because there's always talk of the next big thing at the mine, and most of it comes slower than people say.
S1.think: Privately I think drills would be among the first machines to go automatic, since self-running drills already exist. Being junior, I'd be on the list.
S1.do: Waits to see what the mine actually does before acting. Raises savings from 300 to 400 a fortnight, cuts back on takeaway, and won't look elsewhere until something is in writing.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a worry at the back of her head but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I can feel when the drill bit hits a soft patch through my seat, and a screen can't give me that.
S1.fieldNote: She knows automated drills exist and sees herself at risk, yet her instinct is to wait for something in writing. She would reluctantly take screen training. She doesn't really blame anyone, seeing cost-cutting as just what companies do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's mad, it can't be real. Then I'd stop talking about it, because talking doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd lose my job and the house plan would be gone. Nico's job too, probably, if robots can change tyres. Three years of saving for a deposit, and it'd turn into the money we live on while we work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house fund and keep it as an emergency fund. Cut the phone plan, the streaming, the weekends away. If it got bad we'd give up our rental and move back in with my parents for a bit, they've got the granny flat. I'd apply for whatever help the government put on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit sick. I like knowing what's coming, and this is the opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say he told me to go to the post office like my aunt. Mum would make up the granny flat without saying anything. That's how they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to retrain into something else in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't know what to pick. If AI can do almost anything, then picking a course is just guessing. I'd rather keep the money than spend it on guessing.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and can't be real, then stop talking about it because talking doesn't help. She keeps her reactions out of public view.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd lose my job and the house plan would be gone, with my partner's job at risk too. Three years of deposit savings would become living money.
S2.do: Stops the house fund and treats it as an emergency fund, cutting the phone plan, streaming and weekends away. If it gets bad, moves into her parents' granny flat and applies for government help.
S2.feel: Scared and a bit sick, because she likes knowing what's coming.
S2.quote: Three years of saving for a deposit, and it'd turn into the money we live on while we work out what's next.
S2.fieldNote: The deposit fund turning into survival money was the concrete loss she kept returning to. She refuses to spend on retraining because she sees picking a course as guessing. Her parents are her fallback, described with quiet affection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same, I wouldn't say much. Maybe that we've got a few years, so no point panicking yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to get the deposit, but then what's the point of a mortgage if the job goes? I think I'd keep saving and just not buy. Sit on the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling and keep saving, 400 a fortnight. Put the house on hold until we see what the mine does. Maybe ask HR if there's a maintenance or blast crew opening, since those seem harder for a robot, but I wouldn't push it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than the slow one, less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on buying. How would Nico feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be upset. He's been sending me listings every Sunday. I'd be the one saying no to every house he sends, and I'd hate being that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said blast crew might be harder for a robot. What made you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The blast crew handle explosives, and people get nervous about machines doing that. But I'm only guessing. In five years they'd probably sort that too.

S3.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe that we have a few years so there's no point panicking yet. She prefers to keep her worries to herself.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to save the deposit, but she doubts the point of a mortgage if the job could go. She'd keep saving and not buy.
S3.do: Keeps drilling and saving 400 a fortnight while putting the house purchase on hold. Might ask HR about a maintenance or blast crew opening, but wouldn't push hard.
S3.feel: Anxious, somewhere between the slow and fast pictures.
S3.quote: I'd be the one saying no to every house he sends, and I'd hate being that person.
S3.fieldNote: Her biggest cost here is relational: saying no to every house listing her partner sends. She floated a move to the blast crew but immediately doubted it. She stays cautious and holds cash rather than committing to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can change. That's what my dad says about everything, so I'd probably end up saying it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'd be thirty-seven at the end. That's a long time to keep drilling and saving, and maybe by then I'd have figured out something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like normal for the first few years. We'd probably still buy the house, but a cheaper one so the mortgage is small. I'd keep the savings going and not do anything big until it was clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe you'd have figured out something else. Any idea what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Nico says I should do something with numbers since I log all the depths so neatly. I don't know. Something steady, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in ten years, would you rather the change came early or late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Late, definitely. I'd rather have ten good years drilling than five good years and five years worrying. Even if it ends the same.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can change. That's what my dad says about everything, so I'd probably end up saying it too.
S4.think: Privately she'd be fine for most of it and would be thirty-seven at the end. That's a long time to keep drilling and saving and maybe find something else.
S4.do: Carries on as normal for the first few years. Still buys a house with her partner but picks a cheaper one with a small mortgage, and keeps saving without making any big moves.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly okay.
S4.quote: I'd rather have ten good years drilling than five good years and five years worrying.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her plans go ahead in a smaller, safer form, a cheaper house. She has no clear idea of what she'd do next and doesn't pretend to. Her preference for late change over early warning sums up her outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. I'd want some steady money while we sort things out, from the government or the company, I don't mind which. And someone telling us straight what jobs will actually still be around, so I'm not guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Nico much. Everyone talks about my job, but if his goes too, there's no one in our house earning.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about my job, but if his goes too, there's no one in our house earning.
portrait: Carla Chen is 27 and drills blast holes at the Marrow Creek open-cut coal mine, still learning and still occasionally drilling a row too shallow. She lives with her partner Nico, who works at a tyre shop, and they've been saving 300 a fortnight towards a house deposit. She is quiet, practical, avoids risk and never uses AI, and doesn't really blame anyone for change. She stays calm in the plateau picture, moves to uneasy and then alarmed as change speeds up, and responds every time by saving, holding off on big decisions and waiting for something in writing.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both she and her partner could lose their income with the house deposit turning into living money.
whatWouldHelp: Steady money from the government or the company while they sort things out, and straight information about which jobs will still exist.
